chapter.name: Security
chapter.description: ACLs, Port Security, DHCP Snooping, AAA and switch/network hardening

questions.question: What are the differences between standard and extended ACLs?
questions.answer: Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) filter only by source address, evaluated closest to the destination. Extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) filter by source, destination, protocol, and port (and can use 'established'), evaluated closest to the source.
questions.explanation: Named ACLs can be standard or extended too. Wildcard masks match: 0.0.0.0 = exact host, 255.255.255.255 = any; processing stops at the first matching line.
acceptableAnswers: standard filters by source only, extended by source destination protocol port
standard near destination, extended near source
hints: What does the rule 'least specific location' mean?
Which one can filter by port?

questions.question: How do you place a wildcard mask to match exactly the host 192.168.10.5?
questions.explanation: The wildcard mask bits mark which bits to ignore — all 0s means check every bit. 255.255.255.255 is 'any', 0.0.0.255 is an exact /24.

questions.question: ACL entries are evaluated in order, and the first matching line decides the action — a later 'permit all' does not rescue a packet hit by an earlier deny.
questions.answer: true
questions.explanation: Process order matters absolutely. Any packet that matches an earlier line is immediately permitted or denied; there is no aggregation of rules. Access-control lists implicitly deny everything not explicitly permitted.

questions.question: Write a named extended ACL (SEC-100) that permits HTTP and HTTPS from host 10.1.1.10 to server 10.9.9.9/32 and denies everything else — then apply it inbound on interface Gi0/1.
questions.answer:
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SEC-100
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.1.1.10 host 10.9.9.9 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.1.1.10 host 10.9.9.9 eq 443
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SEC-100 in
questions.explanation: Named ACLs are edited line-by-line with permit/deny statements; the implicit deny is redundant but explicit here for clarity. The interface direction is from the perspective of the router.
acceptableAnswers: named extended acl permitting 80 and 443 for that host pair, applied inbound

questions.question: Which command shows the rules of an access list together with the match counters on every line?
questions.answer: show access-lists
questions.explanation: Counters on each ACE show how many packets matched — use them to find 'shadowed' lines that never match. 'show ip access-lists' shows only IP ACLs.
acceptableAnswers: show access-lists

questions.question: Which command shows the ACLs applied to each interface and the direction they face?
questions.answer: show ip interface (or show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/1)
questions.explanation: Under 'Inbound access list is ...' / 'Outgoing access list is ...' you can see the applied lists; 'show access-lists' then gives the counters per ACE.
acceptableAnswers: show ip interface

questions.question: Users can browse the web but an application server behind the router fails. show access-lists shows deny counts climbing on lines for 10.1.1.0/24. What is the most likely problem?
questions.answer: The ACL is missing a rule for the application's ports/protocol (e.g. TCP 8443 or UDP), or the server's traffic is being denied by an earlier line that accidentally matches — verify the application port in the ACL and check counters against the server IP.
questions.explanation: Deny counters climbing indicate matching packets: check whether the intended traffic is hitting the deny line (wrong port/protocol in the rule) or the rule order.
symptoms: Web traffic works, the application server does not
Deny counters increment on lines affecting the server subnet
No recent config change to the server
questions.topology: Host 10.1.1.50 -> Router Gi0/1 -> App server 10.9.9.99/32 listening on TCP 8443
questions.showOutput:
R1# show access-lists SEC-100
10 permit tcp host 10.1.1.10 host 10.9.9.99 eq 80 (12 matches)
20 permit tcp host 10.1.1.10 host 10.9.9.99 eq 443 (3 matches)
30 permit ip any any (1771 matches)
R1# show access-lists SEC-100
10 permit tcp host 10.1.1.10 host 10.9.9.99 eq 80 (0 matches)
acceptableAnswers: application port not permitted by the acl
deny hit the app traffic
hints: Which traffic is the server expecting?
What does a climbing deny counter mean?

questions.question: What does port security do and what are the three violation modes?
questions.answer: Port security restricts which MAC addresses may send traffic on a switchport. Violation modes: protect (drops frames from unknown MACs, does nothing else), restrict (drops frames AND increments the violation counter, can log), and shutdown (err-disables the port — default and safest).
questions.explanation: Config: switchport port-security maximum N, mac-address sticky/static, violation {protect|restrict|shutdown}. Sticky entries learn dynamically and are stored in config.
acceptableAnswers: restricts macs on the port; protect restrict shutdown
protect drops, restrict drops and counts, shutdown err disables
hints: Which mode actually tears down the port?
What does restrict do that protect does not?

questions.question: A workstation was replaced with one that has a new MAC address. Which violation mode causes the switchport to go into err-disable state when the new MAC sends traffic?
choices: none — port security never disables ports
questions.answer: shutdown (default)
questions.explanation: Limit the max to 2 and use 'errdisable recovery' so the port auto-recovers; or pre-authorize both MACs as sticky/static.

questions.question: Write the commands to enable port security on Gi0/1 with a maximum of 2 MACs and auto-recovery from err-disable in 30 seconds.
questions.answer:
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 2
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation interval 30
questions.explanation: Port security defaults to maximum 1 and violation shutdown; you should also consider 'switchport port-security aging time' for dynamic aging.
acceptableAnswers: port security with max 2 and errdisable recovery

questions.question: Once a switchport has port security enabled with sticky learning, the learned MACs survive a reboot even without being explicitly configured.
questions.answer: false
questions.explanation: No: sticky entries only survive reboots if they were written to the running/startup config with 'write' — the 'sticky' keyword merely converts dynamically learned MACs into config entries that are then saved.

questions.question: Which command shows the port security settings and current secure MACs of an interface?
questions.answer: show port-security interface GigabitEthernet0/1
questions.explanation: Shows max, violation mode, secure MAC addresses, security violation count, and whether the port is in err-disable.
acceptableAnswers: show port-security interface

questions.question: After a violation, which commands both recover the err-disabled port manually?
questions.answer:
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery interval 30
or manually: SW1(config)# interface Gi0/1 ; SW1(config-if)# shutdown ; SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
questions.explanation: The automatic path needs both the cause and an interval (globally). The manual path is shutdown/no shutdown on the interface.
acceptableAnswers: errdisable recovery with the psecure violation cause
shutdown then no shutdown
hints: Which two global commands together auto-recover?
Which manual sequence flips the port?

questions.question: What is DHCP snooping and what are trusted vs untrusted ports?
questions.answer: DHCP snooping filters DHCP messages per port and builds a DHCP snooping binding table (IP + MAC + port + VLAN) to block rogue DHCP servers and spoofed DHCP replies. Trusted ports (uplinks to real DHCP servers) pass all DHCP traffic; untrusted ports (typically towards clients) only permit DHCP Discover/Request — they drop Offer/Ack from anyone.
questions.explanation: Untrusted ports also rate-limit DHCP packets (rate limiter default 15 pps for IOS). The binding table protects against IP/MAC spoofing by validating source IP in later packets.
acceptableAnswers: filters dhcp to block rogue servers; trusted toward server, untrusted toward clients
dhcp snooping builds ip mac port vlan bindings
hints: Which direction is toward the real server?

questions.question: Where do you typically mark ports as TRUSTED in a DHCP snooping design?
choices: Ports connecting to switches or routers upstream, toward the legitimate DHCP server
Only ports in the management VLAN
The ports of the DHCP server's own access device, only if voice VLAN is used
questions.answer: Ports connecting to switches or routers upstream, toward the legitimate DHCP server
questions.explanation: Client-facing ports must be untrusted — otherwise an attacker on a client port could send forged offers which are normally dropped by an untrusted port.

questions.question: Write the commands to enable DHCP snooping for VLAN 10 and mark Gi0/24 (the uplink) as trusted.
questions.answer:
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
questions.explanation: Global enable first, then per-VLAN. Optionally add 'ip dhcp snooping rate-limit' on client ports and 'ip dhcp snooping binding' to statically seed the table.
acceptableAnswers: global snooping, vlan 10, trust on uplink

questions.question: Which command shows the DHCP snooping binding table with IP, MAC, VLAN, and port for each client?
questions.answer: show ip dhcp snooping binding
questions.explanation: Columns: MAC address, IP address, Lease, Type (dhcp-snooping vs static), VLAN, Interface. A stale entry here can cause traffic drops after an IP change.
acceptableAnswers: show ip dhcp snooping binding

questions.question: Which command shows the DHCP snooping configuration summary — VLANs enabled, trusted interfaces, and violation counters?
questions.answer: show ip dhcp snooping
questions.explanation: Lists status (enabled), VLANs with snooping, the rate limit, and every trusted/untrusted interface with packet counters.
acceptableAnswers: show ip dhcp snooping

questions.question: What do the three A's of AAA stand for and what methods servers can provide it?
questions.answer: Authentication (who you are), Authorization (what you can do), Accounting (what you did — logging/tracking). Implemented with RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813) or TACACS+ (TCP 49), plus the local database ('aaa authentication login default local').
questions.explanation: TACACS+ encrypts the whole packet and separates A/A/A steps; RADIUS combines authentication and authorization. aaa new-model activates AAA.
acceptableAnswers: authentication authorization accounting
radius or tacacs plus local database

questions.question: Which AAA protocol separates authentication, authorization, and accounting completely and encrypts the full packet?
questions.answer: TACACS+
questions.explanation: TACACS+ (TCP 49, Cisco) encrypts the entire body and each phase is separate; RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813) encrypts only the password and merges auth + authorization.

questions.question: Before AAA can be used on a Cisco device you must enter the command 'aaa new-model'.
questions.answer: true
questions.explanation: aaa new-model enables all AAA commands; it automatically applies 'aaa authentication login default local' if nothing else is configured.

questions.question: Write the commands to enable AAA on login with a RADIUS server 10.2.2.2 (secret cisco123) and fall back to local authentication.
questions.answer:
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# radius server RADIUS-PROD
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.2.2.2
R1(config-radius-server)# key cisco123
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default group radius local
questions.explanation: The 'default' method list applies to all lines that don't have a named list. Fallback order matters: 'group radius local' tries the server first, then the local DB.
commands: aaa authentication login default group radius local
acceptableAnswers: aaa new model, radius server config, group radius local

questions.question: Name at least four common switch/router hardening measures.
questions.answer: Examples: SSH instead of telnet, disable unused services (http server, snmp if unused), strong passwords (secret not password, maybe type 6/9), login block-for on failed attempts, exec-timeout, banner motd, enable secret with encryption, restrict management (ACL + specific VTY lines), control plane policing, edge port security + DHCP snooping.
questions.explanation: For CCNP focus on: enable secret, vty transport input ssh, exec-timeout, service password-encryption (weak vs type 6), login block-for, no ip http server, ACLs on VTY access.
acceptableAnswers: ssh only, disable http, enable secret, timeout, banner, vty acl
disable unused services and use strong management

questions.question: Which command prevents brute-force SSH attempts on the VTY lines by blocking a source after repeated failed logins?
questions.answer: login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
questions.explanation: This global command temporarily blocks the source IP for 120 s after 3 failed attempts within a 60 s window. Show state: 'show login'. Also relevant: 'ip ssh maxstartups'.
